\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI04-P1-PHY-S2-G7-8, source={Score-I - Test 04 (14 Jan 2022)}, questions={7-8}]
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a nonivasive form of brain stimulation in which a changing magnetic field is used to cause electric current at a specific area of the brain through electromagnetic induction. An electric pulse generator, or stimulator, is connected to a magnetic coil, which in turn is connected to the scalp. The stimulator generates a changing electric current within the coil wich induces a magnetic field; this field then causes a second inductance of inverted electric charge within the brain itself. Transcranial magnetic stimulation is achieved by quickly discharging current from a large capacitor into a coil to produce pulsed magnetic fields between 2 and 3 Tesla in strength. Directing the magnetic field pulse at a targeted area in the brain causes a localized electrical current which can then either depolarize or hyperpolarize neurons at that site.

Some design of circuit for discharing of capacitor through coil uses diode, which is like a current direction controller. Diode allow current in one direction \& not in other.
\bfig{237.5}{SI04_p1_phy_s2_para7_8_1.png}
Circuit for this design is as shown. When switch is closed charged capacitor discharges through inductor coil (L) then diode D$_2$ allows inductor to discharge through large resistance R. Diode D$_1$ prevents LC circuit to produce current in oppsite direction in inductor.
\end{bankpassage}

A special metal S conducts electricity without any resistance. A closed wire loop, made of S, does not allow any change in flux through itself by inducing a suitable current to generate a compensating flux. The induced current in the loop cannot decay due to its zero resistance. This current gives rise to a magnetic moment which in turn repels the source of magnetic field or flux. Consider such a loop, of radius $a$, with its center at the origin. A magnetic dipole of moment $m$ is brought along the axis of this loop from infinity to a point at distance $r$ ($\gg a$) from the center of the loop with its north pole always facing the loop, as shown in the figure below.\\
The magnitude of magnetic field of a dipole $m$, at a point on its axis at distance $r$, is $\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3}$, where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. The magnitude of the force between two magnetic dipoles with moments, $m_1$ and $m_2$, separated by a distance $r$ on the common axis, with their north poles facing each other, is $\dfrac{km_1m_2}{r^4}$, where $k$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions. The direction of this force is along the line joining the two dipoles.
\bfig{147.4}{SI09_p2_phy_s2_para7_8_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}

\hline
\end{tabular}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII37-P1-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={Score-II - Test 37 (10 Feb 2025)}, questions={9-10}]
Figure shows how the resistance of a resistor and the reactances of an inductor and a capacitor vary with angular frequency $\omega$. Resistance R is independent of frequency, while the reactances X$_L$ and X$_C$ are not. If $\omega=0$, corresponding to a dc circuit, there is no current through a capacitor because $X_C\to\infty$, and there is no inductive effect because $X_L=0$. In the limit $\omega\to\infty$, $X_L$ also approaches infinity, and the current through an inductor becomes vanishingly small; recall that the self-induced emf opposes rapid changes in current. In this same limit, $X_C$ and the voltage across a capacitor both approach zero.

Figure shows an application of the above discussion to a loudspeaker system. Low-frequency sounds are produced by the woofer, which is a speaker with large diameter; the tweeter, a speaker with smaller diameter, produces high frequency sounds. In order to route signals of different frequency to the appropriate speaker, the woofer and tweeter are connected in parallel across the amplifier output. The capacitor in the tweeter branch blocks the low-frequency components of sound but passes the higher frequencies; the inductor in the woofer branch does the opposite.


\par
\bfig{120}{SII37_p1phy_q910_stem.png}\par
\end{bankpassage}

A magnetic dipole of moment $m$ is brought along the axis of this loop from infinity to a point at distance $r$ ($\gg a$) from the center of the loop with its north pole always facing the loop, as shown in the figure below.\par

The magnitude of the force between two magnetic dipoles with moments, $m_1$ and $m_2$, separated by a distance $r$ on the common axis, with their north poles facing each other, is $\dfrac{km_1m_2}{r^4}$, where $k$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions. The value of $\omega$ is $\dfrac{3\pi\mathrm B^2\mathrm L^2}{\alpha\mathrm{mR}}$. The value of $\alpha$ is :- (Neglect self inductance of system.)\par

\begin{bankq}[id=SA32-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score Advanced - Test 32 (08 May 2024)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Faraday and Lenz}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: metal can in a solenoid, linearly increasing field: stress in the can wall | steps: induced emf = k pi r^2; current through a ring from resistivity and cross section; magnetic force on the current in the field gives pressure on the wall; hoop stress; time at which it breaks}]
Consider a metal can placed coaxially inside a long solenoid. The metal can be modelled as a thin cylindrical shell of radius r. The magnetic field due to the solenoid varies with time t as kt where k is a positive constant. The resistivity of the can is $\rho$ and its breaking stress is $\sigma$. Compute the time at which the can breaks.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$t=\dfrac{\sigma\rho}{r^2K^2}$}
\opt{B}{$t=\dfrac{2\sigma\rho}{r^2K^2}$}
\opt{C}{$t=\dfrac{\sigma\rho}{2r^2K^2}$}
\opt{D}{$t=\dfrac{\sigma\rho}{3r^2K^2}$}

A ring of mean radius r and cross-sectional area A is made of a perfectly conducting wire. Inductance L of the ring is so small that inertia of free electrons cannot be neglected in the current building process. The free electron density in the conductor is n, mass of an electron is m and modulus of charge on an electron is e. Initially the ring is placed in a uniform magnetic field with its plane parallel to induction vector $\vec{\mathrm B}$ of the field as shown in the figure. Find the current ring after it is turned through an angle 90$^\circ$.\par

\opt{C}{$i=\dfrac{B\pi r^2}{L+\frac{m\times2\pi r}{ne^2A}}$}
\opt{D}{$i=\dfrac{B\times2\pi r}{L+\frac{m\times\pi r^2}{ne^2A}}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=PS04-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 04 (29 Oct 2023)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Motional EMF}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, working={Printed key.}, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: metal disc pulley with a block and resistance, motional emf | steps: rotating disc has emf B omega a squared over 2 between centre and rim; current through R; magnetic torque opposes motion; terminal speed; energy dissipation; check options | I: the disc is a Faraday disc generator whose torque is proportional to speed | C: terminal speed and power expressions}]
A metallic pulley is in the shape of a disc of radius $a$. It can rotate freely about a horizontal axis passing through its centre. The moment of inertia of the pulley about this axis is $I$. A light string is tightly wrapped around the pulley with its one end connected to a block of mass $M$. The centre of the pulley and its circumference are connected to a resistance $R$ as shown. The contact of resistance at the circumference does not cause any friction. A uniform magnetic field $B$ is switched on which is parallel to the axis of rotation of the pulley (see Figure). The mass $M$ is allowed to fall. Assume that resistivity of the material of the pulley is negligible.
\bfig{77.4}{PS04_p1_phy_s2_q07_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The acceleration of the block of mass $M$ at the instant its velocity becomes $v_0$ is $\dfrac{Mga^2-\dfrac{B^2a^4v_0}{4R}}{I+Ma^2}$.}
\opt{B}{Assuming that the block can fall through a large distance, the terminal speed ($v_T$) that it will acquire is $\dfrac{4MgR}{B^2a^2}$.}
\opt{C}{The rate of change of kinetic energy of the pulley at the instant when the speed of the falling block is $\dfrac{v_T}{2}$ is equal to $\dfrac{IM^2g^2R}{B^2a^2(I+Ma^2)}$.}
\opt{D}{The rate of change of kinetic energy of the pulley at the instant when the speed of the falling block is $\dfrac{v_T}{2}$ is equal to $\dfrac{IM^2g^2R}{2B^2a^2(I+Ma^2)}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=TMAS03-P2-PHY-S1-G1-2, source={TMAS - Test 03 (10 Sep 2023)}, questions={1-2}]
People waiting near the tracks of an electrically driven train have sometimes noticed a tingling if they touch a conducting object, such as a pipe, connected to the ground. What causes the tingling? The reason is that the electrically driven train is connected to power station through overhead lines which carry Alternating Current. Because such current continuously changes direction and strength, the magnetic field it produces in surrounding space also changes in direction and strength. In our body, this produces eddy currents, but it is too small for a person to notice. However, if the person touches a large conducting object, such as a pipe, the current can be large and noticeable.\par
Let us try to understand this phenomena. Suppose that the man is standing vertically and his hand is touching the pipe. The overhead wire is an infinite wire carrying AC. Assume that man, pipe and the ground made a rectangular conducting loop of resistance $500\Omega$, dimensions as shown. The current in overhead wire is $100\sin400t$ (A).
\bfig{91.1}{TMAS03_p2_phy_s1_para1_2_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}
